Therefore, this study investigates the effect of MgO, ZnO, and TiO2 doping (at 0.5 and 1.0 wt%) on the structural and hydration behavior of C3S. Synthesis was performed at 1500 °C for six hours, followed by characterization using X-ray diffraction (XRD), Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), Brunauer–Emmett–Teller (BET) surface area analysis, and isothermal calorimetry. To further assess the catalytic effects of dopant ions on C3S hydration, higher doping levels (4.0 and 8.0 wt%) were also evaluated. The results show that doping promotes stabilization of the T3, M1, and M3 C3S polymorphs. Among the dopants, MgO-enhanced phases exhibited higher intrinsic reactivity. However, despite this increased reactivity, hydration rates were reduced across all systems due to a dual effect: catalytic interactions with the hydration products and the formation of a physical barrier by excess dopant. These findings provide new insights into the design of doped clinker systems for tailored hydration performance.

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: Doping during Portland cement clinker synthesis significantly influences the stabilization and reactivity of tricalcium silicate (C3S) polymorphs. Therefore, this study investigates the effect of MgO, ZnO, and TiO2 doping (at 0.5 and 1.0 wt%) on the structural and hydration behavior of C3S. Synthesis was performed at 1500 °C for six hours, followed by characterization using X-ray diffraction (XRD), Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), Brunauer–Emmett–Teller (BET) surface area analysis, and isothermal calorimetry. To further assess the catalytic effects of dopant ions on C3S hydration, higher doping levels (4.0 and 8.0 wt%) were also evaluated. The results show that doping promotes stabilization of the T3, M1, and M3 C3S polymorphs. Among the dopants, MgO-enhanced phases exhibited higher intrinsic reactivity. However, despite this increased reactivity, hydration rates were reduced across all systems due to a dual effect: catalytic interactions with the hydration products and the formation of a physical barrier by excess dopant. These findings provide new insights into the design of doped clinker systems for tailored hydration performance.

ce:section.ce:para: Doping, the deliberate incorporation of minor quantities of foreign elements or oxides to tailor material properties, is a well-established strategy in diverse industrial sectors, including semiconductor manufacturing and metallic alloy production [1,2].

Recent shifts toward alternative raw materials and alternative fuels in cement manufacture driven by environmental and economic considerations have increased the introduction of minor constituents and trace elements into the kiln system [3–5]. These unavoidable impurities, whether intentionally added or introduced through feedstocks, can significantly affect clinker mineralogy, reactivity, and performance, underscoring the importance of understanding the mechanisms and implications of doping in modern clinker production [2–7].

In the production of tricalcium silicate (C3S), the main phase of Portland cement clinker, the doping technique stabilizes one or more polymorphs at room temperature. In order to use this technique, the type of dopant ion, its content, and the synthesis temperature must be determined. These factors regulate its efficiency [8–14].

To understand the effect of doping on C3S formation, the types of solid solutions formed through this approach must first be considered. These are generally classified as interstitial or substitutional. For interstitial solid solutions, it is essential to assess whether the impurity can be accommodated within existing lattice vacancies at the synthesis temperature or if the interstitial sites are comparable in size to the dopant. In the case of substitutional solid solutions, the physicochemical properties of the dopant must be compatible with those of the host ion to be replaced. Key factors include valence, electronegativity, crystal structure, and unit cell volume [15,16].
The formation of C3S initially involves a solid substitution solution, and as the dopant ion increases, minor defects occur in the lattice, transforming it into an interstitial solution [17,18].

The C3S formed from a substitutional solid solution occurs preferentially with the substitution of the calcium ion from the dopant ion due to the type and length of the chemical bond in comparison to the silicon ion. In the crystal structure of C3S, oxygen (Oc) is bonded to silicon (covalent bond), forming the silicon tetrahedron, with a bond distance ranging from 1.64 to 1.67 Å. In contrast, calcium is bonded (ionic bond) to oxygen (Oi) with a bond distance ranging from 2.33 to 2.48 Å, making it weaker and more susceptible to substitution [19]. Studies show that dopant ions replace calcium ions due to the formation energy required to break the CaO and SiO chemical bonds [20,21].
The interstitial solid solution is more difficult to form due to the energy required to create several vacancies equivalent to the size of the impurity in the crystal structure [20,22].

Dopants can be introduced in various forms, including ions (e.g., Mg2+, Cr3+, Al3+, and Fe2+), oxides (e.g., Cr2O3, ZnO, CuO, NiO, Pb3O4, Al2O3, MgO, P2O5, Mn2O3, SO3, and BaO), or sulfates (e.g., SO4 2−, CaSO4, K₂SO4, and Na₂SO4. Among these, MgO, ZnO, and Al2O3 are the most used dopants. However, a clear correlation between dopant type and the stabilization of a specific polymorph remains elusive. This is largely due to conflicting findings reported in the literature, where the same dopant depending on its concentration can stabilize different polymorphs. Table 1 presents data from the literature on this behavior.

Despite the extensive research on doping in Portland cement clinker synthesis, a clear and consistent relationship between specific dopants and the stabilization of tricalcium silicate (C3S) polymorphs remains elusive. This uncertainty stems from the variability in experimental conditions reported across the literature, including differences in dopant concentrations, synthesis protocols, and thermal treatment parameters. As a result, it is common to find conflicting data where the same dopant stabilizes different polymorphs depending on its concentration and the synthesis route employed.

An example involves ZnO as a dopant. Urabe et al. [11] investigated ZnO additions ranging from 0.8 to 8.0 wt% under a sintering regime of 1500 °C for six hours. The authors reported that 8.0 wt% ZnO stabilized the rhombohedral (R) polymorph, while intermediate concentrations (3.2–6.4 wt%) induced transitions among triclinic (T1, T2) and monoclinic (M1, M3) forms. In contrast, Lv et al. [31] applied lower ZnO contents (0.1–3.0 wt%) at a reduced sintering temperature (1450 °C for two hours, repeated over three cycles) and observed stabilization of the M1 polymorph at lower ZnO contents, with a transition toward the R polymorph at 3.0 wt%. Similarly, Lü et al. [23], using the same conditions as Lv et al. [31], reported a progressive transformation from T1 to M2 and then to R polymorphs as ZnO content increased. However, these studies did not report furnace type or cooling rates factors known to significantly influence polymorphic stabilization, further complicating direct comparisons.

In addition to single dopant systems, research has also explored the combined effects of dopants such as MgO, Na2O, and SO3. Maki et al. [32] conducted a comprehensive study of industrial clinkers from various regions, concluding that MgO content plays a decisive role in determining the dominant phase in hybrid M1/M3 samples. Subsequent work by Staněk and Sulovský [33] demonstrated that increasing the MgO/SO3 ratio favored stabilization of the M3 polymorph, whereas a lower ratio promoted the M1 form. However, Segata et al. [13] suggested that SO₃ alone can stabilize the M1 polymorph, independent of other impurities.

When evaluating C3S reactivity solely based on polymorphic form, literature commonly ranks the T1 polymorph as the most reactive, followed by M1 and then M3 [17,22,34–38]. Nevertheless, this approach oversimplifies the complex interplay between crystal structure and chemical composition. Minor ionic substitutions originating from raw materials or alternative fuels used in co-processing can significantly alter the local structure and reactivity of C3S. Therefore, a more nuanced understanding of C3S hydration must consider both polymorphism and the role of dopant-induced structural modifications.

Despite these insights, the specific role of dopants in modulating C3S reactivity, independent of polymorphic form, and their influence on both anhydrous and hydrated properties remain insufficiently explored. This study, therefore, seeks to systematically investigate the effect of ionic doping on C3S reactivity using a suite of physicochemical techniques, and to propose a framework for understanding dopant-induced reactivity variations in C3S.

Pure tricalcium silicate (C3S) was synthesized using analytical-grade calcium carbonate (CaCO3) and silicon dioxide (SiO2) in a molar ratio of 3:1. For the doped samples, analytical-grade oxides of zinc (ZnO), magnesium (MgO), and titanium (TiO2) were added at concentrations of 0.5 wt% and 1.0 wt%, relative to the total mass of the base materials.

The dry components were manually homogenized, and Milli-Q water was gradually added until a paste-like consistency was achieved. The resulting paste was then molded into cylindrical specimens measuring 2.5 cm in diameter and 5.0 cm in height. These specimens were dried at 100 ± 5 °C for 72 h. Following drying, the samples were sintered at 1500 °C for six hours in a muffle furnace. After sintering, the specimens were rapidly cooled to room temperature within a maximum of two minutes using mechanical ventilation to ensure abrupt quenching. Fig. 1 shows the C3S synthesis setup.

Table 4 show the values (including ASS) and particle size distribution curves for the pure and ZnO, TiO2, and MgO-doped phases, respectively. Doping in all samples contributed to an increasing particle size distribution about Dv90. As the dopant content increased, the Dv90 diameter values also increased, requiring greater grinding energy to maintain the finesses parameters compared to reference. The average diameter also showed, for the most part, an increasing behavior as a function of the dopant content used.

One can note that the specific surface area decreased, as the dopant content increased. This behavior remains constant for the phases doped with ZnO, indicating a possible formation of less porous agglomerates. However, for the phases doped with TiO2 and MgO, the highest value was found at a content of 0.5 wt%, with 5.280 m2/g and 5.976 m2/g, respectively, and with the increase in dopant content, there was a drastic reduction. This behavior could be associated with greater densification of the sample during sintering.

Quantitative phase analysis (Fig. 5 ) revealed that the pure C3S phase consisted predominantly of the triclinic T3 polymorph (98.7 %), with a minor fraction of free lime (f-CaO, 1.3 %). In the ZnO-doped systems, the dominant polymorph shifted toward monoclinic forms. At 0.5 wt% ZnO, the assemblage comprised 92.0 % M1, 6.2 % T3, and 1.9 % f-CaO, whereas at 1.0 wt% ZnO, M1 remained the most abundant phase (68.7 %), accompanied by 29.8 % M3 and 1.5 % f-CaO. For the TiO2-doped compositions, T3 remained predominant, although a partial transition from M1 to T3 was observed at both doping levels. At 0.5 wt% TiO2, the phase distribution was 68.9 % T3, 31.0 % M1, and 0.1 % f-CaO, while at 1.0 wt% TiO2 it was 65.2 % T3, 34.4 % M1, and 0.4 % f-CaO. In MgO-doped samples, T3 and M1 coexisted, with 0.5 wt% MgO yielding 88.7 % T3, 9.5 % M1, and 1.8 % f-CaO, whereas 1.0 wt% MgO produced a more balanced distribution (51.5 % T3, 47.1 % M1, and 1.5 % f-CaO).

As the C3S polymorphs are metastable at room temperature, the polymorph with the highest fraction in each doped system was considered the predominant form for this analysis. The T3/M1 and M1/M3 ratios (Fig. 5) indicate that, under the synthesis and cooling conditions employed, T3 tended to stabilize in most cases, except for the 1.0 wt% ZnO system, where monoclinic polymorphs (M1 and M3) predominated, with M1 as the major phase. This divergence may be attributed to the interplay between sintering and cooling protocols and the intrinsic physicochemical characteristics of the dopant cation.

Triclinic C3S polymorphs are generally more stable at ambient temperature due to their lower transformation temperatures compared to monoclinic and rhombohedral forms [12,41]. It has been shown that slow cooling or forced ventilation after sintering at 1450–1600 °C favors T3 stabilization [10].

However, the literature indicates that dopant-induced phase stabilization is not straightforward. The phase assemblage depends not only on dopant concentration but also on synthesis temperature, dwell time, and cooling regime, often resulting in the coexistence of multiple polymorphs at room temperature as shown in Table 1. Taken together, these results emphasize the complexity of polymorph stabilization in doped C3S. The observed trends suggest that dopant effects are not governed solely by ionic size or charge, but also by their interaction with the evolving silicate lattice during cooling. A comprehensive understanding of these interactions considering both thermodynamic and kinetic factors is essential to link phase stability to hydration reactivity and, ultimately, to cement performance.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Effect of doping on the crystal structure
ce:section.ce:para: The incorporation of these dopants has a marked impact on the crystal structure and polymorphism of C3S. Mg2+, due to its similar ionic radii and high symmetry, can substitute Ca2+ with minimal disruption to the [SiO4]4− framework. The substitution leads to a decrease in unit cell volume and an increase in crystal density, effectively counterbalancing the higher atomic weight of Mg2+ [42]. Moreover, the presence of Mg2+ influences the enthalpy of formation and promotes polymorphic transitions by inducing structural distortions and increased formation energy, which may ultimately reduce MgO solubility [19,21,42,43]. Experimental and literature data confirm that MgO stabilizes a range of polymorphs, predominantly in the triclinic (T2, T3) and monoclinic (M1, M2) forms, within doping ranges of 0.1 wt%–4.0 wt% [13,19,27,32,42,43].

Similarly, Zn2+ tends to substitute for Ca2+ due to the lower CaO bond energy compared to SiO, leading to lattice contraction. However, Zn incorporation is closely tied to the oxygen vacancy dynamics during sintering, and unlike more volatile elements, ZnO remains stable even at high temperatures [45–49]. Excess Zn not incorporated into the C3S lattice tends to form secondary phases that can alter both reactivity and mechanical strength [18,50]. Importantly, ZnO has been found to stabilize all seven known C3S polymorphs, although no consistent correlation between Zn content and specific polymorph stabilization has been established. Doping levels reported in the literature range from 0.1 wt% to 8.0 wt%, with the polymorphic outcome highly dependent on synthesis conditions.

In contrast, the effect of TiO2 on the crystal structure of C3S is less well-defined in the literature. Most studies associate TiO2 with its mineralizing behavior, primarily affecting the liquid phase during sintering. It has been shown to lower the temperature for initial liquid formation, increase melt volume, and enhance reaction kinetics at solid–liquid interfaces [25,52,53]. These phenomena can reduce free CaO and promote C3S formation. However, its incorporation into the C3S crystal structure may be more complex and limited, likely occurring in interstitial positions due to its smaller size and higher charge. Reported polymorphs stabilized by Ti doping include triclinic (T1, T2), monoclinic (M1, M3), and rhombohedral forms, typically at doping levels of 0.5 wt%–2.0 wt% [30,52–55]. Crystallite size.

Another significant effect observed in the doped phases is the average crystallite size among the different polymorphs. The pure phase (T3) exhibited the largest crystallite size, while the introduction of dopants influenced this parameter differently depending on the type and content of dopant. Specifically, phases doped with ZnO and MgO showed an increase in crystallite size as the dopant concentration increased, however, for TiO2, a decrease in crystallite size occurred. Table 7 shows the crystallite sizes of each polymorph.

This behavior suggests a strong link between dopant type and the diffusion mechanisms active during crystal formation. In the case of ZnO and MgO, the primary diffusion mechanism is associated with oxygen vacancies, which are generated during the substitution of Ca2+ by Zn2+ or Mg2+ in the lattice. These substitutional solid solutions allow the crystal structure to evolve in a manner similar to the pure phase. As the dopant content increases, so does the number of vacancies, which in turn enhances ion mobility and supplies the necessary energy to facilitate bond breaking and dopant incorporation ultimately promoting crystal growth.

Additionally, ZnO is known to exhibit anisotropic diffusion behavior [56] which further facilitates directional diffusion and contributes to enhanced crystallite growth. This effect aligns with the observed increase in average crystallite size with ZnO doping.

In contrast, TiO2 forms an interstitial solid solution, where the Ti4+ ions occupy positions within the lattice that are not normally occupied by host ions. If no adjustments are made to the synthesis conditions to accommodate this structural disruption, the presence of interstitial ions can impede lattice rearrangement and crystal growth, effectively blocking the expansion of crystallites. This phenomenon is consistent with the mechanism described by Ma et al. [25], in which the incorporation of Ti4+ in interstitial sites leads to structural hindrance and limited crystallite development.

Fig. 7 shows the behavior of the IR spectra of the C3S polymorphs for the pure and doped phases, and Table 8 shows the vibration bands. The IR absorption spectra formed by C3S can be seen in the 400 to 4000 cm−1 region and present four fundamental vibration modes for the [SiO]4 4− tetrahedra, these being: ν1 symmetrical stretching, ν3 asymmetrical stretching, ν2 in-plane bending and ν4 out-of-plane bending [27,50].

The FTIR spectra of all samples exhibited the characteristic vibrational features of C3S, with band positions and intensities modulated by the type and concentration of dopant. In agreement with previous reports [12,57,58], the undoped C3S phase displayed the symmetric stretching vibration (ν₁) of the [SiO4]4− tetrahedra at 860 and 1012 cm −1, asymmetric stretching modes (ν₃) at 1050 and 1008 cm−1, in-plane bending (ν₂) at 492, 461, 434, and 318 cm−1, and out-of-plane bending (ν₄) at 516 cm−1. The prominent band at 862 cm−1 is indicative of the triclinic T3 polymorph, consistent with the XRD phase identification.

Doping induced measurable shifts in the main SiO stretching bands, suggesting modifications in the silicate lattice through ionic substitution or localized structural distortion. For both 0.5 wt% and 1.0 wt% contents, the ν₃ SiO band shifted slightly toward lower wavenumbers in ZnO-doped and MgO-doped samples compared with TiO2-doped compositions. This downshift is consistent with the larger ionic radii of Zn2+ (0.74 Å) and Mg2+ (0.72 Å) relative to Ti4+ (0.605 Å), which can impose greater lattice strain and alter SiO bond lengths [27,49,50,59]. Similar dopant-induced spectral shifts have been reported for transition-metal-substituted silicates [60], reflecting changes in both bond strength and local symmetry.

The bands at 858–860 cm−1, attributed to Si–O–Si bending vibrations [58], exhibited a subtle increase in intensity and a minor shift in samples doped at 1.0 wt%, irrespective of the dopant type. This behavior suggests modifications in intertetrahedral connectivity, potentially linked to dopant–oxygen coordination and charge-balancing mechanisms. In the 400–500 cm−1 region, the observed lower-wavenumber bands correspond to lattice vibrations involving CaO as well as metal–oxygen bonds such as TiO, ZnO, and MgO [27]. The appearance and intensification of these bands in doped samples provide spectroscopic evidence for dopant incorporation into the C3S crystal structure, corroborating the XRD-derived lattice parameter variations.

These FTIR findings reinforce the conclusion that the doping strategy adopted in this study effectively promoted partial substitution of Ca2+ sites and altered the silicate framework. The extent and nature of these modifications depended on the dopant ionic radii and valence, as well as on the concentration employed, in line with previous work on doped calcium silicates [10,23,31]. When combined with the crystallographic results, the vibrational spectroscopy data confirm that Zn2+ and Mg2+ exert a more pronounced structural perturbation than Ti4+, potentially influencing both phase stability and hydration reactivity.
Fig. 8 presents the heat evolution curves of the C3S pastes, both pure and doped, over the first 72 h of hydration. Panels (a) and (b) correspond to 0.5 wt% and 1.0 wt% dopant contents, respectively.

At a doping content of 0.5 wt%, the MgO-modified C3S phase exhibited the shortest induction period, indicating an earlier onset of hydration. It also presented the highest heat release rate during the acceleration period, with an increase of 34.78 % compared to ZnO (33.81 %), the pure phase (baseline), and TiO2 (70.35 %). When the dopant content was increased to 1.0 wt%, the heat release rate decreased for MgO (29.49 %) and ZnO (20.15 %), whereas TiO2 showed a slight increase (32.43 %). In all cases, MgO and ZnO-doped samples exhibited higher cumulative heat release than both the pure and TiO2 phases.

The enhanced early hydration in the MgO series can be attributed to the partial substitution of Mg2+ for Ca2+ within the C3S crystal lattice. Given the ionic radii of Mg2+ (0.72 Å) and Ca2+ (1.00 Å), the ∼28 % difference falls within the Hume–Rothery limit for solid solution formation, allowing substitution with some lattice relaxation [61]. At low substitution levels, this results in a slight lattice contraction, which increases lattice strain energy and facilitates dissolution upon contact with water, enhancing reactivity [41]. However, at higher MgO contents, the accumulation of substitutions can induce localized stress, generating defects such as oxygen or calcium vacancies to relieve strain [12]. This defect formation may reduce structural stability and partially offset the kinetic benefits.

In the study of 40 industrial clinkers [62] showed that both periclase content and total MgO in the clinker mineralogy were identified as significant parameters influencing hydration after 7 days. The authors bring to discussion that although the literature remains divided regarding the role of MgO in very early hydration (first 24 h) [63,64], several works [43,65,66] reported that MgO incorporation enhances the degree of hydration at later ages. This effect has been attributed to the incorporation of Mg2+ ions into the C3S lattice, which can accelerate alite hydration rates [66]. Additionally, MgO presence has been linked to the promotion of alite formation during clinker synthesis, indirectly influencing subsequent hydration behavior.

Considering the Zn doping, this feature can be explained by the early precipitation of zinc-containing secondary phases, such as Zn(OH)2 [67] or Ca[Zn(OH)3·H2O]3 [68], which sequester Ca2+ from the pore solution and delay its supersaturation, thereby shifting the main C–S–H nucleation event to a later time. The resulting second exothermic peak reflects this delayed growth process. The stabilization of the M1 polymorph in ZnO-doped samples further differentiates their behavior from the T3-based pure and MgO/TiO2 phases, though polymorph stabilization alone does not account for the observed reactivity trends.

Indeed, despite all phases except ZnO sharing the T3 polymorph, the reactivity sequence MgO–T3 > pure T3 > TiO2–T3 indicates that catalytic and electronic effects of dopants are more influential than crystal structure alone. The superior reactivity of M1-stabilized ZnO over TiO2–T3 contradicts conventional trends in C3S polymorph reactivity [26,49]. This observation supports the view that foreign ions modify the hydration process primarily through alterations in defect density, local crystal field, and surface chemistry, which in turn modulate dissolution rates and nucleation kinetics [2,10,18,31,42,44,71–74].

Collectively, the results confirm that dopant type and concentration exert a complex, non-linear influence on C3S hydration, arising from the interplay of structural substitution, secondary phase precipitation, and surface-mediated catalytic effects. This reinforces the need to interpret hydration kinetics in doped systems beyond simple polymorph-based frameworks, integrating both bulk and interfacial chemistry effects.

Catalytic, in the context of cement hydration, refers to the acceleration or retardation of chemical reactions due to the presence of foreign ions or impurities. These species modify the activation energy of the reaction without being consumed and without altering the reaction's equilibrium [75]. Although typically present in low concentrations, dopants can dramatically influence hydration kinetics through structural, chemical, or physical interactions with the host matrix [31,51,71].

ce:section.ce:section-title: Dopant effects at low concentrations (0.5–1.0 wt%)
ce:section.ce:para:
As shown in Fig. 9 , the dopant type significantly alters the hydration kinetics:
•
MgO-doped C3S exhibited the greatest variation in activation energy and the highest cumulative heat release. This behavior is attributed to the formation of structural defects and the inherent high lattice symmetry of MgO, which enhances ionic mobility and facilitates the growth of C-S-H. The dopant likely accumulates at the grain boundaries, enhancing the dissolution rate of C3S and promoting early hydration.
•
ZnO-doped C3S, in contrast, showed limited changes in activation energy and lower heat release, indicating sluggish hydration. This aligns with previous reports [18,48,73,76], and is related to ZnO's hexagonal crystal structure and its anisotropic diffusion behavior. Depending on the crystallographic orientation, ZnO may hinder water penetration and Ca2+ diffusion, thereby retarding the reaction.
•
TiO2-doped C3S showed an initial reduction in activation energy, suggesting faster onset of hydration. However, the total heat release remained lower than that of the pure phase. This paradox is explained by TiO2's interference in C3S crystal growth during synthesis, which leads to a denser microstructure with reduced pore space for ionic diffusion, limiting long-term hydration despite faster initiation.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Dopant effects at higher concentrations (4.0–8.0 wt%)
ce:section.ce:para: The impact of dopant content becomes more pronounced at higher concentrations, as shown in Fig. 10 . Across all dopants, a general reduction in hydration reactivity was observed, marked by delayed induction periods, and diminished heat evolution during the acceleration phase.

MgO-doped C3S showed a marked decline in reactivity at 4.0 wt% and 8.0 wt% doping. Although MgO promotes hydration at lower levels, excessive Mg2+ leads to supersaturation and particle agglomeration on the grain surface, forming a barrier that impedes ion exchange. The heat release during the acceleration phase dropped by 74.04 % (4.0 wt%) and 78.28 % (8.0 wt%), with corresponding delays in hydration onset.

The early heat release peak observed for the 4.0 wt% ZnO-doped C3S during the dissolution/induction period can be attributed to the rapid reaction of excess Zn2+ ions with OH− in the pore solution, forming secondary phases such as Zn(OH)2. This reaction occurs almost immediately upon mixing with water and releases energy associated with the nucleation of these low-solubility phases. Such behavior has been described by Tao et al. [48] and Gineys et al. [45], who showed that early-stage zinc reactions lead to the formation of insoluble compounds that influence the onset and evolution of cement hydration.

ZnO-doped C3S displayed the most dramatic decline in reactivity. At 8.0 wt% ZnO, the induction period extended by ∼30 h, and the acceleration peak nearly vanished. The reduction in reactivity is attributed to the formation of insoluble zinc phases such as Ca[Zn(OH)3·H2O]2 and amorphous Zn(OH)2 during early hydration [48,50,77]. These precipitates scavenge Ca2+ from solution, suppressing supersaturation and delaying C-S-H nucleation.

TiO2-doped C3S also showed significant inhibition at higher contents. The 4.0 wt% TiO2 sample exhibited a 91.98 % reduction in acceleration-phase heat release compared to the 0.5 wt% content. At 8.0 wt%, no distinct hydration stages were observed. This is due to the formation of CaTiO3 a stable, unreactive compound that forms a persistent physical barrier on the grain surface, obstructing water ingress and ion mobility.

The catalytic effect behavior of each dopant can be rationalized as follows:
•
MgO: Enhances hydration through structural modification. Even at concentrations exceeding solubility limits, hydration proceeds due to reduced unit cell volume and high symmetry. Excess MgO accumulates on the grain surface but remains permeable to ionic diffusion, sustaining hydration.
•
ZnO: Acts as a retarder. At low levels (≤1.0 wt%), Zn2+ reduces C3S reactivity by forming insoluble secondary phases, but hydration is still observable. At higher contents, the precipitation of zinc hydroxides forms a barrier layer that significantly limits Ca2+ availability, halting hydration.
•
TiO
2 : At low content, it reduces activation energy and accelerates initial hydration. However, it disrupts C3S crystallization and forms CaTiO3 during synthesis, which inhibits diffusion during hydration. At higher levels, the surface passivation effect dominates, thereby passivating the surface and halting hydration.

This surface-blocking mechanism is common to all dopants at high concentrations. Excess dopant accumulates at the grain interface, forming a protective layer that impairs ion transport and suppresses C-S-H formation. The magnitude and nature of this barrier depend on the dopant's chemistry, solubility, and interaction with Ca2+ and OH− ions in the pore solution, behavior already observed in the study by Xu et al. [73].
